Card.Historical features: ___E:Duffy Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffy_Square)___ ___E:George Michael Cohan statue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_George_M._Cohan)___ ___E:One Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Times_Square)___

Main.sentence: Times Square is a major commercial intersection, tourist destination, entertainment hub, and ___E:neighborhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhoods_in_New_York_City)___ in the ___E:Midtown Manhattan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown_Manhattan)___ section of ___E:New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)___ .

It is formed by the junction of ___E:Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan))___ , ___E:Seventh Avenue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_Avenue_(Manhattan))___ , and ___E:42nd Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(Manhattan))___ .

Together with adjacent ___E:Duffy Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffy_Square)___ , Times Square is a ___E:bowtie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowtie)___ -shaped plaza five blocks long between 42nd and ___E:47th Streets U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_Street_(Manhattan))___ .

Times Square is brightly lit by numerous ___E:digital billboards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_billboard)___ and advertisements as well as businesses offering ___E:24/7 service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24/7_service)___ .

One of the world's busiest pedestrian intersections,  it is also the hub of the ___E:Theater District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater_District,_Manhattan)___ ,  where most ___E:Broadway theatres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre)___ are located, and a major center of the world's ___E:entertainment industry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_industry)___ .
Times Square is one of the world's most visited tourist attractions, drawing an estimated 50 million visitors annually.

Approximately 330,000 people pass through Times Square daily,  many of them tourists,  while over 460,000 pedestrians walk through Times Square on its busiest days.  The ___E:Times Square–42nd Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square%E2%80%9342nd_Street_station)___ and ___E:42nd Street–Port Authority Bus Terminal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street%E2%80%93Port_Authority_Bus_Terminal_station)___ stations have consistently ranked as the busiest in the ___E:New York City Subway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway)___ system, transporting more than 200,000 passengers daily.

Formerly known as Longacre Square , Times Square was renamed in 1904 after The New York Times moved its headquarters to the then newly erected Times Building, now ___E:One Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Times_Square)___ .

It is the site of the annual New Year's Eve ___E:ball drop U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_Ball)___ , which began on December 31, 1907, and continues to attract over a million visitors to Times Square every year,  in addition to a worldwide audience of one billion or more on various ___E:digital media U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media)___ platforms.

Times Square, specifically the intersection of Broadway and 42nd Street, is the eastern terminus of the ___E:Lincoln Highway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Highway)___ , the first road across the United States for motorized vehicles.

Times Square is sometimes referred to as "the Crossroads of the World",  "the Center of the Universe",  and "the heart of ___E:the Great White Way U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan)#Great_White_Way)___ ".
Times Square functions as a ___E:town square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_square)___ , but is not geometrically a ___E:square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square)___ .

It is closer in shape to a bowtie, with two triangles emanating roughly north and south from 45th Street,  where ___E:Seventh Avenue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh_Avenue_(Manhattan))___ intersects ___E:Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan))___ .

Broadway similarly intersects other north–south avenues at ___E:Union Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Square_(Manhattan))___ , ___E:Madison Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Square_and_Madison_Square_Park)___ , ___E:Herald Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herald_Square)___ , and ___E:Verdi Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verdi_Square)___ , none of which are squares.

The area is bounded by West ___E:42nd Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(Manhattan))___ , West ___E:47th Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_Street_(Manhattan))___ , 7th Avenue, and Broadway.

Broadway runs diagonally, crossing through the horizontal and vertical ___E:street grid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_grid)___ of Manhattan laid down by the ___E:Commissioners' Plan of 1811 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioners%27_Plan_of_1811)___ , and that intersection creates the "bowtie" shape of Times Square.
Times Square is the official name of the southern triangle, below 45th Street.

The northern triangle is officially known as ___E:Duffy Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duffy_Square)___  and was dedicated in June 1939 to honor World War I chaplain Father ___E:Francis P. Duffy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_P._Duffy)___ of the ___E:69th New York Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/69th_New_York_Infantry_Regiment)___ .
A statue by ___E:Charles Keck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Keck)___ was dedicated in May 1937 as a memorial to Duffy.

There is also ___E:a statue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statue_of_George_M._Cohan)___ of composer and entertainer ___E:George M. Cohan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_M._Cohan)___ ,   and the ___E:TKTS U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TKTS)___ discount ticket booth for same-day Broadway and off-Broadway theaters that has been at the site since June 1973.

When ___E:Manhattan Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Island)___ was first settled by the ___E:Dutch colonists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_colonization_of_the_Americas)___ , three small streams united near what is now the intersection of ___E:10th Avenue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10th_Avenue_(Manhattan))___ and ___E:40th Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40th_Street_(Manhattan))___ .
These three streams formed the "Great Kill" (Dutch: Grote Kil ).

From there the Great Kill wound through the low-lying Reed Valley, known for fish and waterfowl,  and emptied into a deep bay in the ___E:Hudson River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River)___ at the present 42nd Street.
The name was retained in a tiny hamlet, Great Kill, that became a center for carriage-making, as the upland to the south and east became known as Longacre.

Before and after the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ , the area belonged to ___E:John Morin Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Morin_Scott)___ , a general of the ___E:New York militia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_militia)___ , in which he served under ___E:George Washington U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington)___ .
Scott's ___E:manor house U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manor_house)___ was at what is currently 43rd Street, surrounded by countryside used for farming and breeding horses.

In the first half of the 19th century, it became one of the prized possessions of ___E:John Jacob Astor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jacob_Astor)___ , who made a second fortune selling off lots to hotels and other real estate concerns as the city rapidly spread ___E:uptown U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Manhattan)___ .
By 1872, the area had become the center of New York's horse carriage industry.

The locality had not previously been given a name, and city authorities called it Longacre Square after ___E:Long Acre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Acre)___ in London, where the horse and carriage trade was centered in that city.  ___E:William Henry Vanderbilt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Vanderbilt)___ owned and ran the American Horse Exchange there.
In 1910, it became the Winter Garden Theatre.

As more profitable commerce and industrialization of ___E:Lower Manhattan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan)___ pushed homes, theaters, and ___E:prostitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostitution)___ northward from the ___E:Tenderloin District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenderloin,_Manhattan)___ , Longacre Square became nicknamed the Thieves Lair for its increasingly prominent reputation as a low entertainment district.

The first theater on the square, the ___E:Olympia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Theatre_(New_York_City))___ , was built by cigar manufacturer and ___E:impresario U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impresario)___ ___E:Oscar Hammerstein I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Hammerstein_I)___ .

According to Gotham: A History of New York City to 1898 , "By the early 1890s this once sparsely settled stretch of Broadway was ablaze with electric light and thronged by crowds of middle- and upper-class theatre, restaurant and cafe patrons."

In 1904, New York Times publisher ___E:Adolph S. Ochs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolph_Ochs)___ moved the newspaper's operations to a new skyscraper on 42nd Street at Longacre Square, on the site of the former ___E:Pabst Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pabst_Hotel)___ , which had existed on the site for less than a decade since it opened in November 1899.  Ochs persuaded Mayor ___E:George B. McClellan Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._McClellan_Jr.)___ to construct a ___E:subway station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_%E2%80%93_42nd_Street_(New_York_City_Subway))___ there, and the area was renamed "Times Square" on April 8, 1904.  Just three weeks later, the first electrified advertisement appeared on the side of a bank at the corner of 46th Street and Broadway.
The north end later became Duffy Square, and the former Horse Exchange became the ___E:Winter Garden Theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Garden_Theatre)___ , constructed in 1911.

The New York Times moved to more spacious offices one block west of the square in 1913 and sold the building in 1961.  The old Times Building was later named the ___E:Allied Chemical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allied_Corp.)___ Building in 1963.  Now known simply as ___E:One Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Times_Square)___ , it is famed for the ___E:Times Square Ball drop U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_Ball)___ on its roof every New Year's Eve.

In 1913, the ___E:Lincoln Highway Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Highway_Association)___ , headed by entrepreneur ___E:Carl G. Fisher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_G._Fisher)___ , chose the intersection of 42nd Street and Broadway (at the southeast corner of Times Square) to be the Eastern Terminus of the ___E:Lincoln Highway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Highway)___ .

This was the first road across the United States, which originally ran 3,389 mi (5,454 km) coast to coast through 13 states to its western terminus in ___E:Lincoln Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Park_(San_Francisco))___ in San Francisco.
Times Square grew dramatically after ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ .
It became a cultural hub full of theatres, ___E:music halls U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_hall)___ , and upscale hotels.

Times Square quickly became New York's ___E:agora U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agora)___ , a place to gather to await great tidings and to celebrate them, whether a World Series or a presidential election.
— ___E:James Traub U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Traub)___ , The Devil's Playground: A Century of Pleasure and Profit in Times Square
___E:Advertising U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertising)___ also grew significantly in the 1920s, growing from $25 million to $85 million over the decade.

For example, the ___E:Wrigley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Company)___ Spearmint Gum sign, possibly the biggest electric sign "in the world," cost $9,000 per month to rent.  Some contemporary critics, such as ___E:Thorstein Veblen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thorstein_Veblen)___  and ___E:G. K. Chesterton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._K._Chesterton)___ ,  disliked the advertising at Times Square. ___E:Fritz Lang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Lang)___ , after seeing Times Square in 1923, used it as inspiration for his dark industrial film Metropolis .

Entertainment icons such as ___E:Irving Berlin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irving_Berlin)___ , ___E:Charlie Chaplin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chaplin)___ , and ___E:Fred Astaire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Astaire)___ were closely associated with Times Square in the 1910s, 1920s, and 1930s.

However, it was also during this period that the area began to be besieged by crime and corruption, in the form of gambling and prostitution; one case that garnered huge attention was the arrest and subsequent execution of police officer ___E:Charles Becker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Becker)___ .
The general atmosphere of Times Square changed with the onset of the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ in the early 1930s.
City residents moved uptown to cheaper neighborhoods, and many popular theaters closed, replaced by saloons, brothels, "burlesque halls, vaudeville stages, and dime houses".
The area acquired a reputation as a dangerous and seedy neighborhood in the following decades.
Nevertheless, Times Square continued to be the site of the annual ___E:ball drop on New Year's Eve U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_Ball)___ .

The ball drop was placed on hiatus for New Year's Eve in 1942 and 1943 due to lighting restrictions during ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , replaced by a moment of silence that was observed at midnight in Times Square, accompanied by the sound of chimes played from sound trucks.

On May 8, 1945, a massive crowd celebrated ___E:Victory in Europe Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_in_Europe_Day)___ in Times Square;  and on August 15, 1945, the largest crowd in the history of Times Square gathered to celebrate ___E:Victory over Japan Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_over_Japan_Day)___ , reaching an estimated two million.

The victory itself was announced by a headline on the "zipper" ___E:news ticker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_ticker)___ at ___E:One Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Times_Square)___ , which read "OFFICIAL ***TRUMAN ANNOUNCES JAPANESE SURRENDER ***".

From the 1960s to the early 1990s, the seediness of the area, especially due to its ___E:go-go bars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go-go_bar)___ , ___E:sex shops U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_shop)___ , ___E:peep shows U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peep_show)___ , and adult theaters, became an infamous symbol of the city's decline.
As early as 1960, 42nd Street between Seventh and Eighth avenues was described by The New York Times as "the 'worst' [block] in town".
Later that decade, Times Square was depicted in Midnight Cowboy as gritty, depraved, and desperate.

Conditions only worsened in the 1970s and 1980s, as did the ___E:crime U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_in_New_York_City)___ in the rest of the city, with a 1981 article in Rolling Stone magazine calling 42nd Street in Times Square the "sleaziest block in America".

In the mid-1980s, the area bounded by 40th and 50th Streets and Seventh and Ninth Avenues saw over 15,000 crime complaints per year.  The block of 42nd Street between Seventh and Eighth avenues had 2,300 crimes per year in 1984, of which 20% were felonies.
Times Square was known in the 1970s-80s as the most notorious area for prostitution.

In this era, formerly elegant movie theaters began to show ___E:x-rated films U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_rating)___ , and ___E:peep shows U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peep_show)___ hustlers were common.
In 1984, the area was so derelict and dilapidated, that the entire Times Square area paid the city only $6 million in property taxes (equivalent to $18.2 million in 2024).

In the 1980s, a commercial building boom began in the western parts of Midtown as part of a long-term ___E:development plan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_plan)___ developed under mayors ___E:Ed Koch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Koch)___ and ___E:David Dinkins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Dinkins)___ .

These included office buildings such as ___E:1540 Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1540_Broadway)___ , ___E:1585 Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1585_Broadway)___ , and ___E:750 Seventh Avenue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/750_Seventh_Avenue)___ , as well as hotels such as the ___E:Macklowe Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Times_Square_New_York)___ , ___E:Marriott Marquis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Marriott_Marquis)___ , ___E:Crowne Plaza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crowne_Plaza_Times_Square_Manhattan)___ , and DoubleTree Suites.

By 1986, ___E:New York City Planning Commission U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Planning_Commission)___ (CPC) was considering enacting regulations that would have forced new buildings along Times Square to include bright signage as well as deep ___E:setbacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setback_(architecture))___ .

The CPC adopted a planning regulation in 1987, which required large new developments in Times Square to set aside about 5 percent of their space for "entertainment uses".  [a] The regulation also required new buildings on Times Square to include large, bright signs.

The buildings at 1540 Broadway, 1585 Broadway, and 750 Seventh Avenue were completed at the beginning of the ___E:early 1990s recession U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_1990s_recession)___ , when 14.5 percent of Manhattan office space was vacant.
Furthermore, some 9 ×10 ^ 6 sq ft (840,000 m 2 ) of office space in the western section of Midtown had been developed in the 1980s, of which only half had been leased.

Consequently, 1540 Broadway was completely empty, while 1585 Broadway and 750 Seventh Avenue had one tenant each, despite the buildings having over 2 ×10 ^ 6 sq ft (190,000 m 2 ) of office space between them.   Entertainment conglomerate ___E:Bertelsmann U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann)___ bought 1540 Broadway in 1992,   spurring a revival of Times Square in the early 1990s.
This was hastened when financial firm ___E:Morgan Stanley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley)___ bought 1585 Broadway in 1993,  followed by 750 Seventh Avenue in 1994.

The ___E:Empire State Development Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Development_Corporation)___ (ESDC), an agency of the New York state government, had proposed redeveloping the area around a portion of West 42nd Street in 1981.  Four towers designed by ___E:Philip Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Johnson)___ and ___E:John Burgee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Burgee)___ were to be built around 42nd Street's intersections with ___E:Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan))___ and Seventh Avenue.

These towers would have been redeveloped by George Klein of Park Tower Realty, though the ___E:Prudential Insurance Company of America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prudential_Insurance_Company_of_America)___ joined the project in 1986.    Furthermore, as part of the West Midtown special zoning district created in 1982, the New York City government had allowed new buildings in Times Square to be developed with an increased floor area ratio.
To ensure the area would not be darkened at nightfall, the city passed zoning regulations that encouraged developers to add large, bright signs on their buildings.

In 1990, the ___E:State of New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state))___ took possession of six of the nine historic theaters on 42nd Street, and the ___E:New 42nd Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_42nd_Street)___ ___E:non-profit organization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization)___ was appointed to oversee their restoration and maintenance.
The theaters underwent renovation for Broadway shows, conversion for commercial purposes, or demolition.

Opposition to the towers on Times Square, along with Prudential and Park Tower's inability to secure tenants for the proposed buildings,  led government officials to allow Prudential and Park Tower to postpone the project in 1992.   By then, Prudential had spent $300 million on condemning the sites through ___E:eminent domain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain)___ .
The partners retained the right to develop the sites in the future,  and the ESDC's zoning guidelines remained in effect.
In exchange for being permitted to delay construction of the sites until 2002, Prudential and Park Tower were compelled to add stores and install large signage on the existing buildings.

In 1992, the Times Square Alliance (formerly the Times Square ___E:Business Improvement District U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Improvement_District)___ , or "BID" for short), a coalition of city government and local businesses dedicated to improving the quality of commerce and cleanliness in the district, started operations in the area.  In 1998, the alliance opened a tourist information center in the former ___E:Embassy Theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_Theatre_(New_York_City))___ at 1560 Broadway;  the information center operated until 2014.

In the mid-1990s, Mayor ___E:Rudolph Giuliani U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_Giuliani)___ led an effort to clean up the area, an effort that is described by Steve Macek in Urban Nightmares: The Media, the Right, and the Moral Panic Over the City : Security was increased, pornographic theatres were closed, and "undesirable" low-rent residents were pressured to relocate, and then more tourist-friendly attractions and upscale establishments were opened.
Advocates of the ___E:remodeling U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remodeling)___ claim that the neighborhood is safer and cleaner.

Detractors have countered that the changes have homogenized or ___E:"Disneyfied" U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyfication)___ the character of Times Square and have unfairly targeted lower-income New Yorkers from nearby neighborhoods such as ___E:Hell's Kitchen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell%27s_Kitchen,_Manhattan)___ .

The changes were shaped in large part by the actions of ___E:The Walt Disney Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company)___ , which bought and restored the ___E:New Amsterdam Theatre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam_Theatre)___ after several attempts at redevelopment had failed.

As part of a contract with Disney, officials from the city and state evicted the pornographic theaters and contracted with ___E:Madame Tussauds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madame_Tussauds)___ and ___E:AMC Theatres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMC_Theatres)___ to move onto 42nd Street.
This spurred the construction of new office towers, hotels, and tourist attractions in the area.

Prudential and Klein dissolved their partnership for the four office-building sites at Times Square's southern end in 1996.   The same year, ___E:Douglas Durst U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Durst)___ acquired the site at the northeast corner of Broadway and 42nd Street,  and he developed ___E:4 Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Times_Square)___ there.

The northwest corner of Seventh Avenue and 42nd Street was taken by ___E:Reuters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters)___ , which enlisted ___E:Rudin Management U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudin_Management)___ as its development partner and built ___E:3 Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3_Times_Square)___ on that corner;   that building opened in 2001.  In 1998, a joint venture of Klein, ___E:The Blackstone Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blackstone_Group)___ , and ___E:Boston Properties U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Properties)___ won the right to acquire the sites at the southwest and southeast corners of 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue for $330 million.   ___E:5 Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5_Times_Square)___ was completed on the southwest-corner site in 2002,   and ___E:Times Square Tower U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_Tower)___ opened on the southeast-corner site in 2004.

Times Square now boasts attractions such as ___E:ABC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company)___ 's ___E:Times Square Studios U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Square_Studios)___ , where Good Morning America is broadcast live; competing ___E:Hershey's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hershey_Company)___ and ___E:M&M's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%26M%27s)___ stores across the street from each other, and multiple multiplex movie theaters.

Additionally, the area contains restaurants such as the ___E:Bubba Gump Shrimp Company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubba_Gump_Shrimp_Company)___ , a ___E:seafood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seafood)___ establishment; ___E:Planet Hollywood Restaurant and Bar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planet_Hollywood)___ , a ___E:theme restaurant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theme_restaurant)___ ; and Carmine's, serving ___E:Italian cuisine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_cuisine)___ .
It has also attracted several large financial, publishing, and media firms to set up headquarters in the area. A larger presence of police has improved the safety of the area.

The theatres of Broadway and the huge number of animated ___E:neon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neon_sign)___ and ___E:LED U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED)___ signs have been one of New York's iconic images as well as a symbol of the intensely urban aspects of Manhattan.

Since 1987 such signage has been mandated by ___E:zoning ordinances U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoning_ordinance)___ that require building owners to display illuminated signs, the only district in New York City with this requirement.
The neighborhood has a minimum limit for lighting instead of the standard maximum limit.
The density of illuminated signs in Times Square rivals that in ___E:Las Vegas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas)___ .
Officially, signs in Times Square are called "spectaculars", and the largest of them are called " ___E:jumbotrons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumbotron)___ ".

This signage ordinance was implemented in accordance with guidelines set in a revitalization program that New York Governor ___E:Mario Cuomo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo)___ implemented in 1993.

Notable signage includes the ___E:Toshiba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshiba)___ billboard directly under the NYE ball drop, the curved seven-story ___E:NASDAQ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASDAQ)___ sign at the ___E:NASDAQ MarketSite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASDAQ_MarketSite)___ at ___E:4 Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Times_Square)___ on 43rd Street, and the curved ___E:Coca-Cola sign U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca-Cola_sign)___ located underneath another large LED display owned and operated by ___E:Samsung U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung)___ .
Both the Coca-Cola sign and Samsung LED displays were built by LED display manufacturer ___E:Daktronics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daktronics)___ .

Times Square's first environmentally friendly billboard powered by wind and solar energy was first lit on December 4, 2008.  The new ___E:20 Times Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20_Times_Square)___ development hosts the largest LED signage in Times Square at 18,000 square feet.  The display is 1,000 square feet larger than the Times Square ___E:Walgreens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walgreens)___ display and one of the largest ___E:video-capable screens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_video_screens)___ in the world.

In 2002, New York City mayor ___E:Rudy Giuliani U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani)___ administered the oath of office to the city's next mayor, ___E:Michael Bloomberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg)___ , at Times Square after midnight on January 1 as part of the 2001–02 New Year's celebration.
Approximately 500,000 revelers attended.

Security was high following the ___E:September 11 terrorist attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_terrorist_attacks)___ in 2001, with more than 7,000 ___E:New York City police officers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Police_Department)___ on duty in the Square, twice the number for an ordinary year.
Times Square started hosting other major annual events in the 2000s.
Since 2002, the summer solstice has been marked by "Mind over Madness", a mass yoga event involving up to 15,000 people.
Tim Tompkins, a co-founder of the event, said part of its appeal was "finding stillness and calm amid the city rush on the longest day of the year".

Architect ___E:Mark Foster Gage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Foster_Gage)___ proposed and designed the original Times Square Valentine's Day heart in 2009. Since then, designing the heart has become an annual competition.

In February 2011, Times Square became smoke-free as New York extended the outdoors ___E:smoking ban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_smoking_bans_in_the_United_States)___ to the area. The measure imposed a $50 fine for any person caught smoking within the area.  From January 29 to February 1, 2014, a "Super Bowl Boulevard" was held on Broadway, especially in Times Square, between 34th and 47th Streets, as part of ___E:Super Bowl XLVIII U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLVIII)___ .

The boulevard contained activities such as autographs, a 60 ft (18 m)-high ___E:toboggan run U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toboggan_run)___ , and photographs with the ___E:Vince Lombardi Trophy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vince_Lombardi_Trophy)___ .
The area was under increased security and witnessed over 400,000 people during the period.

In October 2022, casino operator ___E:Caesars Entertainment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesars_Entertainment)___ and commercial property developer ___E:SL Green U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SL_Green)___ submitted a joint proposal to open a ___E:casino U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino)___ at ___E:1515 Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1515_Broadway)___ , along Times Square.
The community advisory committee rejected the proposal in September of 2025, therefore ending the prospects of a ___E:casino hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casino_hotel)___ in Times Square.

On February 26, 2009, Mayor ___E:Michael Bloomberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg)___ announced that traffic lanes along ___E:Broadway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_(Manhattan))___ from ___E:42nd Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(Manhattan))___ to 47th Street would be de-mapped starting Memorial Day 2009 and transformed into pedestrian plazas as a trial until at least the end of the year. The same was done in ___E:Herald Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herald_Square)___ from 33rd to 35th Street.
The results were to be closely monitored to determine if the project was successful and should be extended.

Bloomberg also stated that he believed the street shutdown would make New York more livable by reducing pollution, cutting down on pedestrian-vehicle accidents, and helping traffic flow more smoothly through the Midtown street grid.
The pedestrian plaza project was originally opposed by local businesses, who thought that closing the street to cars would hurt business.

The original seats put out for pedestrians were inexpensive multicolored plastic lawn chairs, a source of amusement to many New Yorkers; they lasted from the onset of the plaza transformation until August 14, 2009, when they were ceremoniously bundled together in an installation christened Now You See It, Now You Don't by the artist Jason Peters, and shortly afterward were replaced by sturdier metal furniture.

Although the plaza had mixed results on traffic in the area, injuries to motorists and pedestrians decreased, fewer pedestrians were walking in the road, and the number of pedestrians in Times Square increased.
On February 11, 2010, Bloomberg announced that the pedestrian plazas would become permanent.

The city started rebuilding the plaza in 2010, hiring the design and landscaping firm ___E:Snøhetta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sn%C3%B8hetta_(company))___ to permanently replace Broadway's roadway with custom-made granite pavers and benches.

By December 2013, the first phase of the Times Square pedestrian plaza had been completed at the southern end of the square in time for the Times Square Ball drop on New Year's Eve.  The project was originally intended to be completed by the end of 2015.  The entire project was finally completed just before New Year's Eve 2016.  Some safety ___E:bollards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollard_(traffic))___ were also installed as part of the renovation to prevent ___E:vehicular attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle-ramming_attack)___ or ___E:collisions U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_collision)___ on the sidewalk.
After ___E:a 2017 vehicle-ramming attack U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Times_Square_car_attack)___ , there were calls to install more bollards along Times Square.

Times Square's pedestrian plaza is frequented by ___E:topless U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toplessness)___ women (with painted breasts) called " ___E:desnudas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desnuda)___ ", as well as ___E:costumed characters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costumed_characters)___ , who typically ___E:panhandle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begging)___ for tips.  The pedestrian plaza became a source of controversy in the summer of 2015 because of a large number of complaints about the topless women and panhandling characters.

Although neither of these activities are illegal, opponents believed that the panhandlers' presence was detrimental to the ___E:quality of life U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_of_life)___ in the area.  There were calls from Police Commissioner Bratton and Mayor ___E:Bill de Blasio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_de_Blasio)___ to remove the plaza, although Manhattan Borough President ___E:Gale Brewer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale_Brewer)___ opposed the proposal.
In June 2016, work started on "pedestrian flow zones" where no one was allowed to loiter, as well as "activity zones" where costumed characters were allowed to perform.

Times Square is the most visited place globally with 360,000 pedestrian visitors a day, amounting to over 131 million a year.  As of 2013 [update] , it had a greater attendance than each of the ___E:Disney theme parks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_theme_parks)___ worldwide, with 128,794,000 visitors between March 2012 and February 2013, versus 126,479,000 for the ___E:Walt Disney World U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World)___ theme parks in ___E:Bay Lake, Florida U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_Lake,_Florida)___ , in 2012.   Even excluding residents from the visitor count, Times Square is the world's second most visited tourist attraction, behind the ___E:Las Vegas Strip U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas_Strip)___ .

The high level of pedestrian traffic has resulted in $4.8 billion in annual retail, entertainment, and hotel sales,  with 22 cents out of every dollar spent by visitors in New York City being spent within Times Square.

Times Square is the site of the annual New Year's Eve ball drop. About one million revelers crowd Times Square for the New Year's Eve celebrations, more than twice the usual number of visitors the area usually receives daily.

However, for the millennium celebration on December 31, 1999, published reports stated approximately two million people overflowed Times Square, flowing from Sixth Avenue to Eighth Avenue and back on Broadway and Seventh Avenue to 59th Street, making it the largest gathering in Times Square since August 1945 during ___E:celebrations marking the end of World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_over_Japan_Day)___ .
On December 31, 1907, a ball signifying New Year's Day was first dropped at Times Square,  and the Square has held the main New Year's celebration in New York City ever since.

On that night, hundreds of thousands of people congregate to watch the ___E:Waterford Crystal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterford_Crystal)___ ball being lowered on a pole atop the building, marking the start of the new year. It replaced a lavish fireworks display from the top of the building that was held from 1904 to 1906 but stopped by city officials because of the danger of fire. Beginning in 1908, and for more than eighty years thereafter, Times Square sign maker ___E:Artkraft Strauss U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artkraft_Strauss)___ was responsible for the ball-lowering.
During World War II, a minute of silence, followed by a recording of church bells pealing, replaced the ball drop because of wartime blackout restrictions.
Today, Countdown Entertainment and One Times Square handle the New Year's Eve event in conjunction with the Times Square Alliance.

A new energy-efficient LED ball debuted for the arrival of 2008, which was the centennial of the Times Square ball drop. The 2008–09 ball is larger and has become a permanent installation as a year-round attraction, being used for celebrations on days such as ___E:Valentine's Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentine%27s_Day)___ and ___E:Halloween U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween)___ .
The New Year's Eve celebrations are usually overseen by thousands of police officers.
Aluminum barriers are erected to accommodate spectators; for the 2020 celebration, attended by a million people, barriers were erected from 38th to 59th Street and from Sixth to Eighth Avenue.
Typically, the celebrations create large amounts of waste.

The waste includes the 3,000 pounds of ___E:biodegradable U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodegradation)___ ___E:confetti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confetti)___ dropped at midnight, a tradition of which started in 1992.  The ___E:New York City Department of Sanitation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Department_of_Sanitation)___ estimated that by 8 a.m. on New Year's Day 2014, it had cleared over 50 short tons (45 long tons; 45 t) of trash from the New Year's celebration, using 190 workers from their crews and the Times Square Alliance.
The onset of the ___E:COVID-19 pandemic in New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_New_York_City)___ during 2020 reduced the number of people traveling to Times Square.
About 108,000 pedestrians visited Times Square each day in late 2020 compared to the 380,000 before the pandemic.
From March to October 2020, 26 of the area's 46 hotels closed, as well as 39 of 151 stores and 84 of 162 restaurants.
Times Square was closed to the public for New Year's Day 2021 and observers were dispersed into enclosures measuring 8 by 8 ft (2.4 by 2.4 m).

An immediately recognizable location, Times Square has been featured countless times in literature, films, video games, music videos, and on television.
The seediness of the area was featured prominently in such films as Midnight Cowboy (1969),  Born to Win (1971),  and Taxi Driver (1976).

The area was shown in the 1980 film Times Square , which featured a ___E:punk rock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock)___ / ___E:new wave U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music)___ soundtrack.
It was also depicted in the 2011 movie New Year's Eve .

The area also appeared on The Amazing Race as the starting location in a race around the world in the first episode of the show's ___E:25th season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Amazing_Race_25)___ ,  as well as on the ___E:sixth season U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HaMerotz_LaMillion_6)___ of the ___E:Israeli edition of The Amazing Race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HaMerotz_LaMillion)___ with teams finishing their second leg in Times Square.

Times Square has been fictionally attacked and destroyed in several movies, including Knowing , when a ___E:solar flare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_flare)___ destroys New York City;  Deep Impact , when a ___E:tsunami U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami)___ created from a ___E:meteor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteor)___ impact destroys New York City; the 1998 film Godzilla , where Godzilla is chased through Times Square; the Ghostbusters movies; Stephen King's The Stand , where the intersection is overcome by total anarchy; Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen , Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs , and 2012 .
It was also seen in the festival battle scene in the 2002 film Spider-Man , and a stand-off in the later film The Amazing Spider-Man 2 .

Films and TV shows have also employed the opposite tactic, depicting the typically bustling area as eerily still, such as in Vanilla Sky,  as well as the post-apocalyptic I Am Legend , in which ___E:Will Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith)___ and his dog go hunting for deer in the deserted urban canyon.
In the pilot episode of the TV series Blindspot , Times Square is completely emptied due to an abandoned bag being suspected to be a bomb.
Times Square also has featured prominently in video games.
